Publication-Ready Display of DMAR Result Tables

Source: R/dmar_output_helpers.R
dmar_output_helpers.Rd

The dmar_tbl print layer formats a result table for the console. These helpers carry the same formatting into the two places a researcher writes up an analysis: a knitted report and a results sentence.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'dmar_tbl'
knit_print(x, ...)

as_kable(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'dmar_tbl'
as_kable(x, format = NULL, ...)

results_sentence(x, label = NULL, digits = 2, term = NULL, conf_level = NULL)

Arguments

x

A dmar_tbl object (a data.frame returned by a DMAR function). For results_sentence, a dmar_tbl that carries a confidence interval, either as ci_lower / ci_upper rows of a long table or as ci_lower / ci_upper columns of a one-row wide table, such as one row of common_method_adjusted_r or of a tidy() result, or as <estimate>_ci_lower / <estimate>_ci_upper rows beside the estimate's row, as in a sem_fit_measures table, or as <estimate>_ci_lower / <estimate>_ci_upper columns beside the estimate's column of a one-row wide table, as in one row of ci_eta_squared or ci_omega_squared.

...

Additional arguments. For knit_print.dmar_tbl and as_kable.dmar_tbl, passed to kable (other than caption, which as_kable writes itself).

format

Passed to kable as its format argument (for example "html", "latex", "pipe"). The default NULL lets knitr choose based on the output context.

label

For results_sentence, the label that leads the sentence (for example "Cohen's d"). The default NULL uses the name of the point-estimate term: the estimate's row of a long table, the quantity a tidy() row names in its estimand column (see dmar_tidiers), the row's term beside a wide table's estimate or value column, and otherwise the estimate column's name.

digits

For results_sentence, the number of decimal places for the estimate and the interval limits. Default 2. Like the digits of the table display (see dmar_tbl), it counts decimal places, but it keeps a default of its own and does not follow options(dmar.digits = ), so a sentence written for a manuscript does not change with the console display. As in the table, a value that rounds to zero is written without a minus sign (0.00, not -0.00).

term

For results_sentence, the estimate whose interval a table holds in <term>_ci_lower and <term>_ci_upper rows, for example "gamma_hat" in a sem_fit_measures table or "rmsea" in a fa_confirmatory table, or in columns of those names, for example "eta_squared_total" in a row of ci_eta_squared. The default NULL reads the table's interval as described above, taking the first estimate with such rows when the table holds its interval in no other form, and, of such columns, the one estimate whose limits are not NA (a row with several is refused unless term names one). Either way the interval for the standardized mean difference that cles and nnt_from_smd echo beside their own, which theirs are computed from, is taken only when term is "smd".

conf_level

For results_sentence, the confidence level of the table's interval, for a table that records none (one assembled by hand, say). The default NULL reads the level the table records and refuses a table that records none, rather than assuming one; a value that differs from the level the table records is refused.

Value

knit_print.dmar_tbl returns a knit_asis object (the rendered table) for knitr to place in the document. as_kable returns a knitr_kable object. results_sentence returns a length-one character string.

Details

knit_print.dmar_tbl is the knitr print method, so a dmar_tbl dropped into an R Markdown chunk renders as a formatted kable (values to a fixed number of decimal places, whole-number sample sizes without decimals, p-values to fixed decimals) rather than as unrounded doubles. as_kable is the explicit form of the same rendering: it returns the knitr_kable object so the caller can pipe it into further styling or embed it in a larger document. Both show the table the console shows, formatted by format.dmar_tbl (for most results the whole table; for a few, such as fraction_missing_information, which leaves out the columns that carry nothing for the call, and factor_scores, which shows the first rows of each factor, the same view the console prints), together with every line the console writes with it: the sum-of-squares type, the confidence level, how an omega's denominator was estimated and its largest residual correlation, the bootstrap replication counts, the missing data a sample size plan assumed, and the lines a result of its own adds (which version of a fit measure was reported and why, what a model comparison checked, how a fraction of missing information was estimated, which rule set a table of degrees of freedom). What a reader sees in a report therefore matches what they saw at the console, and neither rounds the stored numbers. knit_print.dmar_tbl sets each of those lines as its own paragraph beneath the table (a line that introduces the table, as the summary of factor_scores, the measurement structure of fa_confirmatory, and the model summary of mediation_mbco do, comes before it, and a small table among the lines is set as a code block so its columns stay aligned), and sets the whole off with a blank line before and after it, so that two tables printed in one chunk stay apart; as_kable joins them into the table's caption. Both write those lines in the markup of the format knitr renders the table in, escaped for LaTeX (a document knitted from .Rnw, or format = "latex") and for HTML, so that the percent sign of a confidence level or an underscore in an item name prints as itself; knitr escapes a table's cells and column names but writes a caption as it is given.

results_sentence turns a table that carries a confidence interval into the one sentence an author puts in a results section, for example “smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.10, 0.90]”. It reads the estimate and its limits from the numeric columns at full precision and formats them for the sentence, so the reported numbers are exact to the requested decimals rather than transcribed from the rounded console display. In a wide table the estimate is the column the row names in an estimand column, as the glance() row of a long table names the column of the estimate its interval belongs to (see dmar_tidiers), else the estimate (or value) column when there is one, and otherwise the first numeric column that is not a limit, a standard error, a test statistic with its degrees of freedom and p-value, or a count; a p-value the table carries is appended, to the four decimals of format_p, and one below that floor as the bound it is (“p < 0.0001”). In a long table, whose interval is held in ci_lower and ci_upper rows, the estimate is the row the table names as the one the interval belongs to, when it names one (the corrected correlation of correction_for_attenuation, whose table lists the observed correlation first, and the proportion of superiority of proportion_of_superiority, listed after the standardized mean difference it is computed from), and otherwise its first row that is not a limit. Its p-value is likewise the row the table names as the p-value of its test, when it names one, and otherwise its first p-value row: the equivalence tables of equivalence_r, equivalence_smd, and equivalence_c list the p-values of the two one-sided tests first and name the TOST p-value, the test their \(1 - 2\alpha\) interval decides. A long table may instead hold an estimate's interval in rows of its own, named for the estimate: sem_fit_measures reports rmsea beside rmsea_ci_lower and rmsea_ci_upper, and gamma_hat and adjusted_gamma_hat the same way. The sentence then reports the estimate named by term, or the first such estimate in the table (the RMSEA there), with no p-value, since the p-values of such a table belong to other tests (of exact, close, and not close fit). term also reaches the RMSEA rows of a fa_confirmatory table. The confidence level is the interval's own level when the table records it (fa_confirmatory() records the level of its RMSEA interval, its rmsea_conf_level, in the rmsea_ci_level row and in an attribute of the same name, which is read when a selection of rows leaves that row out; a table stacked with rbind() keeps the attributes of its first table only, so keep the rmsea_ci_level row in each selection when stacking tables fit at different levels), and otherwise the table's conf_level attribute, or its conf_level row or column (as the reliability coefficients and the tidy() and glance() verbs carry it). The tidy() of a long table holds the level in a conf_level column on the rows of its interval, the estimate and the two limits, and NA on the others; the sentence reads the level and the estimate from those rows, so that rows of several tidy() results stacked with rbind() give the sentence of their own table (a frame's attributes are those of the first frame of a stack). Every DMAR table that forms an interval records its level, and a sentence states no level the table does not record: a table that records none, such as one assembled by hand, is refused unless conf_level gives the level its interval was formed at, and a conf_level that differs from the level the table records is refused.

A table whose two limits are not a confidence interval gets a sentence that says so. vargha_delaney_A, cliff_delta, and probability_of_superiority_paired report both limits equal to the estimate when the estimated variance is 0 (completely separated groups, or no variation) and record the case in the table's interval_degenerate attribute. The sentence then gives the estimate and the reason and no interval, “A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the groups are completely separated, so the estimated variance is 0)” or “A = 0.50 (no confidence interval: every score is equal, so the estimated variance is 0)”, with “every pair favors the same member” and “every pair is tied” for the paired function. A p-value is appended only when the table has one (the permutation test of vargha_delaney_A). The tidy() and glance() rows of these tables carry the mark in a logical column interval_degenerate, which says that the variance is 0 and not which case gave it, so their sentence reads “A = 1.00 (no confidence interval: the estimated variance is 0)”.

The level a sentence states is the interval's coverage, which for an interval formed from tail areas alpha_lower and alpha_upper is \(1 - \alpha_{lower} - \alpha_{upper}\) whatever the split. A sentence in the form “95% CI [L, U]” is read as the equal-tailed interval, so an interval whose tail areas differ says so, “smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.03, 0.85] (unequal tail areas: 0.01 below, 0.04 above)”, and an interval with a tail area of 0 is written as the one-sided confidence bound it is, “smd = 0.50, one-sided 95% upper confidence bound 0.83”, since its other limit is infinite or the bound of the parameter (0 for an RMSEA or a squared multiple correlation) and carries no information. The split is read from the table's record of it, never from a limit: an equal-tailed interval whose lower limit is 0 because the statistic fell below its critical value (Steiger, 2004) is written as the two-sided interval it is. The line beneath a printed table states the same split, for example “Confidence level: 95% (unequal tail areas: 0.01 below the lower limit, 0.04 above the upper limit)”, and the tidy() and glance() rows of such an interval carry it in alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns (see dmar_tidiers).

A confidence set that is not an interval is written as what it is. The Fieller set of ci_ratio_of_means and ci_ratio_of_means_paired can be the complement of an interval or the whole line, and with unequal tail areas an interval unbounded on one side or the union of two intervals. The sentence reads the form from the table's confidence_set attribute (or the confidence_set column of its tidy() row) and the ends of the excluded gap from its excluded_lower and excluded_upper rows (or columns), and writes, for example, “ratio = 0.32, 99.5% confidence set: every value except those between 0.90 and 147.05”, “ratio = 0.32, 99.9% confidence set: the whole line, which excludes no value”, or “ratio = 0.32, 97.8% confidence set: the union of [-0.61, 0.93] and [9.55, Inf) (unequal tail areas: 0.02 below, 0.002 above)”, since “99.5% CI [-Inf, Inf]” would read as the whole line and hide the gap. An infinite end is written open and a finite one closed. A bounded Fieller interval is written as any other interval.

A table whose limits are NA, because no interval was formed (as from krippendorff_alpha without a bootstrap), has no sentence to write and gives an error.

References

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

See also

dmar_tbl for the console print layer and format_p for the p-value convention these helpers reuse.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

x <- ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 50, n_2 = 50)

# A knitr_kable that keeps every column, ready for a report.
as_kable(x)
#> 
#> 
#> Table: Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> |term     |value |
#> |:--------|:-----|
#> |ci_lower |0.101 |
#> |smd      |0.500 |
#> |ci_upper |0.897 |

# The sentence an author writes in a results section.
results_sentence(x, label = "Cohen's d")
#> [1] "Cohen's d = 0.50, 95% CI [0.10, 0.90]"

# Wide tables (one interval per row) work the same way.
results_sentence(ci_R2(R2 = 0.25, N = 100, p = 5))
#> [1] "R2 = 0.25, 95% CI [0.08, 0.37]"

# So does one row of a tidy() result, here the same interval.
results_sentence(generics::tidy(x))
#> [1] "smd = 0.50, 95% CI [0.10, 0.90]"

# A table that holds an interval in rows named for its estimate: the
# RMSEA of a model with chi square 85.3 on 24 df and N = 301, with its
# 90 percent interval (the default level of every RMSEA interval), and
# then gamma hat.
fm <- sem_fit_measures(chisq = 85.3, df = 24, N = 301, p = 9)
results_sentence(fm, label = "RMSEA", digits = 3)
#> [1] "RMSEA = 0.092, 90% CI [0.072, 0.114]"
results_sentence(fm, term = "gamma_hat", digits = 3)
#> [1] "gamma_hat = 0.957, 90% CI [0.935, 0.973]"
